title: ULTIMATE HYPERTROPHY PROGRAMS (Novice to Advanced)
summary: NH presents five connected free programs meant to be run in sequence so lifts and volume progress without program hopping. They are beginner (2 sets) and novice (3-day full body), a 4-day bridge with an arm day, a 5-day intermediate upper/lower plus arms, and an advanced 6-day upper/lower x3 with weekly exercise rotations and floating rest days. He explains when to move up, why supersets keep sessions short, and why low sets per session with high frequency is the way to grow.
claims: Program hopping is a plague that can cost years of progress; run connected programs in sequence so lifts and volume progress continuously
His original novice program is three years old and he no longer likes much of it; his philosophy has changed
A six-day template cannot be programmed like a three-day one
Any lift can be swapped for another in the same family; 'or' means pick one and stick with it (novice/intermediate) or rotate weekly (advanced)
Stick with one variation of big compounds; isolation lifts can be rotated because neurological adaptation matters less
Keep the prescribed rep ranges and frequency; changing too much throws the volume off
The final goal is to program for yourself; after years on these programs, take the reins
Full body is the best split for novices: enough high-intensity stimulus and lots of recovery; novices lack physical and mental stamina for long sessions
Novice program: three full-body days (Mon/Wed/Fri) with 48 h between sessions, supersets throughout, two to three compounds per day and the rest isolation
Novices only need one heavy squat and one heavy hinge per week; mid-week legs get lighter split squats, curls and extensions
There is no conventional deadlift in the program because it is not optimal for hypertrophy (C tier); RDLs or barbell rows instead
His previous novice program had too many pull-ups; now they are fewer, weighted when possible, not max reps
Beginner version: same as novice but two sets per exercise and no variations, for those intimidated by volume
Move up a program when you can do and want more volume to keep progressing or you start to plateau
Most people quit at the intermediate stage because they jump from low-volume novice programs to compound-heavy ones; a bridge program builds work capacity first
Bridge: four days with a new arm day, four sets on the first half of the week and three on the rest
Volume drives growth only if intensity stays high; only quality sets count
Evolving rep ranges: max out the rep range on three sets, add a fourth set, then add weight and return to three sets with fewer reps
The upper back is a glutton for volume and needs intense, frequent training, so it gets hit almost every day
You've crossed the bridge when you still have energy after upper days and need four sets per body part to grow; add frequency rather than junk volume per session
Intermediate: upper/lower x2 plus an arm day (five days), sessions of 1 to 1h20 thanks to supersets
Upper days get more exercises than lower days (about 7 vs 6) because isolation matters as much as compounds for upper-body aesthetics, while lower days focus energy on big squats and hinges
The more you train per week, the less volume per session and the less time in the gym
Stay about six months on the beginner program, a year on novice, a year on the bridge and two years on intermediate; milk them
Advanced: six days, upper/lower x3, rotating variations weekly to dodge adaptation, rest days taken whenever recovery requires
Jumping into the advanced program without built-up work capacity will fail; it must be earned
Calf finisher: after heavy seated calf raises, do 3-4 sets to failure with a dumbbell on the knees and feet close together
Never more than two exercises per body part per day on the advanced program
He trains six days a week with 7-8 exercises per session, like the advanced program
Training each muscle three times a week at high intensity, 9-15 hard sets per body part per week is enough to keep growing forever
If weight on the bar stops increasing for good on this program, something is wrong; progress slows but should never stop
Doing 8-12 sets per body part in one session costs frequency and intensity; low sets per session suits high-frequency training
exercises: forearm isolation that also hits biceps
weighted if possible, not max reps
alternative hinge for more upper back
dumbbell on knees, feet close together
